entry: City (pop., 2019: 2,415,266), capital of [[Burkina Faso]]. It is the country's largest city and its administrative, communications, cultural and economic center, with food processing and textiles as its main industries. Possibly founded as early as 1050 by the Soninke Wangara diaspora from the [[Ghana Empire]], it became the main center of the Mossi States when the Wagadugu Kingdom was founded in the 15th century. On 5 September 1896 French forces entered the city and burned it to the ground. In 1919 the colonial administration made it capital of Upper Volta. A railroad from [[Ivory Coast]] reached the city in 1954, and it remains linked by rail to [[Abidjan]]. Its market, one of West Africa's largest, burned in 2003 and reopened with better fire-prevention measures. On 15 January 2016 gunmen attacked central Ouagadougou, killing 28 people.

Catholic title of the Virgin Mary, associated with four apparitions to Juan Diego and one to his uncle, Juan Bernardino, reported in December 1531, when the Mexican territories were part of the [[Spanish Empire]]. The venerated image on the cloak is enshrined in the Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe in [[Mexico City]]. Pope Leo XIII granted a decree of canonical coronation for the image in 1887, and Pope Paul VI raised the shrine to minor basilica status in 1976. Historian Stafford Poole argues that the apparition story coalesced in the 17th century without 16th-century evidence.

Ancient symbol of a serpent or dragon eating its own tail, used to represent the eternal cycle of life, renewal and rebirth. The name derives from Greek words meaning "tail" and "eating." One of its earliest known appearances is in the *Enigmatic Book of the Netherworld*, an Egyptian funerary text from the tomb of [[Tutankhamun]] in the 14th century BCE, where it encircles a figure that may represent the unified [[Ra]]-[[Osiris]]. The symbol was later adopted in [[Gnosticism]], [[Hermeticism]] and [[Alchemy]]. The alchemical *Chrysopoeia of Cleopatra* bears the inscription "hen to pan" ("the all is one").

Senegalese film director, producer and writer, often called the father of African film. Born in Ziguinchor, in Casamance, to a fisherman, he worked at manual jobs in [[Dakar]] before serving in the French Army during [[World War II]]. In [[Marseille]] he worked on the docks and joined the communist-led CGT trade union. His debut novel, *Le Docker Noir* (1956), follows an African stevedore who is executed after accidentally killing a white woman who had stolen his novel, a story reminiscent of [[Albert Camus]]'s *The Stranger*. He turned to film in 1960, and his short *Borom Sarret* (1963) was the first fiction film by a sub-Saharan African. His features, largely in Wolof, include *Mandabi* (1968) and *Xala* (1975). *Ceddo* (1977) was banned in Senegal, and *Moolaadé* (2004) condemned [[Female genital mutilation]].

Remote, vast, sparsely populated interior of [[Australia]], more remote than the area Australians call the bush. Its climates range from tropical and monsoonal in the north to arid in the red center and semi-arid and temperate in the south. Low population density, a largely intact natural environment and pastoralism (livestock grazing) unify the region. [[Aboriginal Australians|Aboriginal peoples]] have lived there for at least 50,000 years, and many hold Traditional Owner status over large parts of it under native title law. European exploration was sporadic. From 1858 to 1861 John McDouall Stuart led six expeditions north from [[Adelaide]] and reached the north coast without losing any of his party. The Overland Telegraph line followed his route in the 1870s. The Outback is recognized globally as one of the largest remaining intact natural areas on Earth.

Art made by self-taught individuals who are untrained in the traditional arts and have little contact with the conventions of the art world. The term was coined in 1972 by critic Roger Cardinal as an English equivalent of *art brut* ("raw art"), a label that Jean Dubuffet created in the 1940s for art made outside official culture. Dubuffet focused on outsiders such as [[Psychiatric hospital|psychiatric hospital]] patients, hermits and spiritualists. Interest in the art of the mentally ill grew from the late 19th century, and members of Der Blaue Reiter group, including [[Wassily Kandinsky]], admired its expressive power. In 1922 Hans Prinzhorn published *Bildnerei der Geisteskranken* (*Artistry of the Mentally Ill*), which drew the attention of [[Paul Klee]] and [[Max Ernst]]. Adolf Wölfli, a psychiatric patient in Switzerland, produced an illustrated epic of 45 volumes narrating his imaginary life story, with 25,000 pages and 1,600 illustrations.

Chinese historian, essayist, poet and statesman of the [[Song dynasty]]. Born in [[Sichuan]], he was largely self-taught after his father died when he was three, and the writings of [[Han Yu]] strongly influenced him. He passed the jinshi examination in 1030 on his third attempt. As a historian he led the compilation of the *New Book of Tang*, completed in 1060, and privately wrote the *Historical Records of the Five Dynasties*. He revived the Classical Prose Movement begun by two [[Tang dynasty]] masters and promoted it in imperial examinations, paving the way for [[Su Shi]]. His prose, including *Zuiwengting Ji*, earned him his greatest acclaim. He supported the Qingli Reforms of the 1040s, and after reform leader Fan Zhongyan fell from power in 1045 he too was demoted. He retired in 1071 after vehemently opposing the New Policies of Wang Anshi, whose career he had helped.

Paired female [[Sex organ|sex organ]], or gonad, lying on either side of the [[Uterus|uterus]]. The ovaries produce oogonia, which develop into immature [[Egg cell|egg cells]] (oocytes) and release a mature egg cell at ovulation. Each oocyte is surrounded by granulosa cells, forming an ovarian follicle. The ovary is also an endocrine gland, producing [[Estrogen|estrogen]] and progesterone, which drive the development of the female reproductive organs and of secondary sex characteristics at [[Puberty]]. The ovaries connect to the uterus through the fallopian tubes and are held in place by ligaments. Each has an outer cortex containing follicles and an inner medulla of blood vessels, nerves and stroma, enclosed by a capsule of dense fibrous tissue. The ovary develops through many stages, from the prenatal period through [[Menopause]].

Large family, *Furnariidae*, of small suboscine [[Passerine|passerine]] birds found from [[Mexico]] through Central America to southern [[South America]]. The family contains around 321 species in 71 [[Genus|genera]]. Its name comes from the elaborate clay nests built by horneros, which resemble ovens; most other ovenbirds build stick nests or nest in tunnels or rock clefts. Furnariid nests always have a cover, and up to six eggs are laid. Birds range from 9 to 35 cm long and occupy habitats from city parks to Amazonian lowlands and Andean highlands. Woodcreepers were merged into the family after analysis of DNA sequences, although some scientists keep them separate. The North American ovenbird (*Seiurus aurocapilla*) is a wood warbler, not a member of this family.

Collective name for 13 French territories outside [[Europe]], mostly remnants of the [[French colonial empire]] that remained part of France after decolonization. Its five overseas regions have the same status as metropolitan regions. The territories lie in the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian oceans, and French Guiana is on the [[South America|South American]] continent. Their land area, excluding Adélie Land in Antarctica, is 120,396 sq km, or 18.0% of France's land territory. Residents, numbering 2,891,000 in January 2026, are mostly citizens of France and the [[European Union]], so they can vote in French and European elections.

Roman poet, a younger contemporary of [[Virgil]] and [[Horace]]. Full name Publius Ovidius Naso. Born in Sulmo, in an Apennine valley east of [[Rome]], to an equestrian family, he studied rhetoric in Rome before renouncing law to pursue poetry. His early work was elegiac poetry on erotic themes, including *Amores* and *Ars Amatoria* (*The Art of Love*). His most famous work, *Metamorphoses*, is a continuous mythological narrative in fifteen books of dactylic hexameter and remains one of the most important sources of classical [[Myth|mythology]]. Quintilian considered him the last of the Latin love elegists. [[Augustus]] exiled him to Tomis, on the [[Black Sea]], where he spent the last nine or 10 years of his life. Ovid attributed his banishment to *carmen et error* ("a poem and a mistake"), and scholars have speculated about the error. His poetry was much imitated in [[Late antiquity|Late Antiquity]] and the [[Middle Ages]].

Member of the order Strigiformes, comprising over 200 mostly solitary, nocturnal [[Bird|birds]] of prey. Owls have large, forward-facing eyes, a flat face and a facial disc of feathers that funnels sound to asymmetrically placed ears. Their feathers are adapted for silent flight. Their eyes are fixed in their sockets, so owls can rotate their heads as much as 270°; they have 14 neck vertebrae, while humans have seven. The smallest species, the elf owl, weighs as little as 31 g. The largest females of the [[Eurasian eagle-owl]] and Blakiston's fish owl reach 71 cm in length and a 190 cm wingspan. Most owls hunt small [[Mammal|mammals]], [[Insect|insects]] and other birds, though a few species specialize in [[Fish|fish]]. Owls are found in all regions of the Earth except the polar ice caps and some remote islands. A group of owls is called a parliament.

Large bovine trained as a draft animal, usually a castrated adult male of [[Cattle|cattle]]. Oxen are commonly castrated because [[Castration|castration]] inhibits [[Testosterone|testosterone]] and aggression, which makes them docile and safer to work with. They are used for plowing, hauling carts and wagons, threshing grain, and powering grain mills or irrigation, and they are usually yoked in pairs. Oxen are thought to have first been harnessed around 4000 BC. The word derives from a reconstructed [[Indo-European languages|Proto-Indo-European]] root translated as "male animal."

Simplest [[Carboxylic acid|dicarboxylic acid]], (COOH)₂. Its name comes from early investigators who isolated it from wood-sorrels of the genus *Oxalis*. It is a white crystalline solid that occurs naturally in plants such as [[Rhubarb]] and [[Spinach]]. It is much stronger than [[Acetic acid|acetic acid]] and is used to remove [[Rust|rust]], because it forms a water-soluble iron complex. Industrially it is made by oxidizing [[Glucose|carbohydrates]] such as glucose with nitric acid or air, at about 120,000 metric tons a year. In 1824 [[Friedrich Wöhler]] obtained it by reacting cyanogen with ammonia. It can be toxic when ingested in significant quantities.

Principal historical dictionary of the [[English language]], published by Oxford University Press, a publishing house of the [[University of Oxford]]. Work began in 1857, and fascicles were published from 1884 under the title *A New English Dictionary on Historical Principles*. The title *The Oxford English Dictionary* was first used on the covers in 1895 and fully adopted in the 1933 reprint. The second edition of 1989 comprised 20 volumes and 21,728 pages. Entries present each sense in order of its earliest recorded use, followed by illustrative quotations in chronological order. As of January 2026 the dictionary contained 520,779 entries, 888,251 meanings and 3,927,862 quotations. A third edition has been compiled since 2000 and is expected to be electronic only. The online version has been available since 2000.

Cathedral city and county town of Oxfordshire, [[England]]. It is home to the [[University of Oxford]], the oldest university in the English-speaking world. Its industries include motor manufacturing, publishing and information technology. The population was 165,940 in 2025. Teaching began in the 11th century, and in 1209 a townsperson's hanging of two scholars led academics to flee and found [[Cambridge]] University. During the [[English Civil War]], Charles I made Oxford his de facto capital. The city lies 56 miles (90 km) northwest of [[London]], at the confluence of the [[River Thames|Thames]] and Cherwell rivers.

Chemical compound containing at least one oxygen atom and one other element. Oxides are extraordinarily diverse, and most of the [[Earth's crust|Earth's crust]] consists of them. Even metals often develop an oxide coating: aluminum foil forms a thin layer of Al₂O₃ that protects it from further oxidation. Most elements form oxides of more than one stoichiometry, such as [[Carbon monoxide|carbon monoxide]] and carbon dioxide. Many metal oxides form when other compounds decompose; heating [[Limestone|limestone]] releases carbon dioxide and leaves [[Calcium oxide|calcium oxide]]: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. Noble metals such as [[Gold]] and [[Platinum]] are prized because they resist combining with oxygen. The chemical produced on the largest scale, [[Sulfuric acid|sulfuric acid]], is made by oxidizing sulfur to sulfur dioxide and then to sulfur trioxide.

Semi-synthetic [[Opioid|opioid]] for moderate to severe pain, sold as Roxicodone and OxyContin. It was first produced in 1916 in [[Germany]] from the opium poppy alkaloid thebaine, and first used medically there in 1917. It acts by activating the μ-opioid receptor, and taken by mouth it has roughly 1.5 times the effect of the same amount of [[Morphine]]. Common side effects include euphoria, constipation, nausea and drowsiness. It is highly [[Addiction|addictive]] and commonly abused. Abuse-deterrent versions combine it with [[Naloxone|naloxone]]. In 2023 it was the 49th most commonly prescribed medication in the United States, with more than 13 million prescriptions.

[[Peptide]] hormone and neuropeptide, produced in the hypothalamus and released by the posterior [[Pituitary gland|pituitary]]. Oxytocin stimulates uterine contractions during [[Childbirth|childbirth]] and milk ejection during lactation, and it plays roles in social bonding, love and reproduction. Its release is controlled by positive feedback: release during a contraction stimulates further release, intensifying labor until the stimulus ceases. Its name derives from Greek words meaning "sharp" and "childbirth," and it is colloquially called the "love hormone." In 1953 Vincent du Vigneaud synthesized it, the first polypeptide hormone to be synthesized, and he won the [[Nobel Prize]] in Chemistry in 1955. Intranasal oxytocin has shown mixed results in trials for [[Autism|autism]], and it is being studied for anxiety disorders.

Former Yoruba empire in [[West Africa]], located in present-day western [[Nigeria]] and [[Benin]]. It grew into the largest Yoruba-speaking state through administrative organization, trade and the military use of [[Cavalry|cavalry]]. From the late 16th to the early 18th century it was among the most politically important states in West Africa, holding sway over most other Yoruba kingdoms and over the Fon Kingdom of Dahomey. According to legend, Ọranmiyan, a prince of Ile-Ife, founded Oyo where a snake disappeared into the ground. The Alaafin was a sacred king, and a council of nobles could compel him to commit [[Suicide|suicide]] if he was judged tyrannical. Around 1535 the Nupe occupied Oyo and drove the dynasty into exile in Borgu. It returned in the early 17th century as a more centralized state.

Common name for several families of saltwater bivalve mollusks that live in marine or brackish habitats. True oysters, family Ostreidae, include the edible oysters, such as the European flat oyster and the Pacific oyster, and they are a major aquaculture product, with global production exceeding 5 million metric tons a year. Oysters breathe mainly through [[Gill|gills]]. A small, three-chambered [[Heart|heart]] pumps colorless blood, and two [[Kidney|kidneys]] remove waste. There is no evidence that oysters have a brain. Pearl oysters belong to the family Pteriidae and are not closely related to true oysters. They make [[Pearl|pearls]] by covering an irritant with nacre. Cultured pearls have far outgrown natural pearls in the market since the early 20th century. The largest pearl-bearing oyster, *Pinctada maxima*, is roughly the size of a dinner plate.

Highland region of the central United States, covering most of southern [[Missouri]] and northern [[Arkansas]]. At nearly 47,000 square miles (120,000 sq km), it is the largest highland region between the [[Appalachia|Appalachians]] and the [[Rocky Mountains|Rockies]]. Its highest point, Wahzhazhe Summit, rises to 2,561 feet (781 m). Together with the Ouachita Mountains it forms the U.S. Interior Highlands. The name derives from the French *aux Arcs*, an abbreviation of *aux Arkansas*, which referred to the trading post at Arkansas Post. Branson, Missouri, just north of the Arkansas border, is a [[Tourism|tourist]] destination where Ozark culture is popularized.

Triatomic [[Oxygen|oxygen]] molecule (O₃), a pale-blue gas with a pungent odor. It is much less stable than dioxygen (O₂) and is formed from it by ultraviolet light and electrical discharges. Christian Friedrich Schönbein noticed the smell after [[Lightning|lightning]] and named the gas in 1839 from the Greek for "to smell." Most ozone lies in the [[Stratosphere|stratosphere]], where it absorbs most of the Sun's [[Ultraviolet|ultraviolet]] radiation. At ground level, above about 0.1 ppm, it damages mucous and respiratory tissues. As a powerful oxidizing agent, ozone is used as a disinfectant and bleach, but concentrated gas and liquid can decompose explosively. Its O₃ structure was determined in 1865.

Decline in the total amount of [[Ozone|ozone]] in Earth's [[Stratosphere|stratosphere]], including the seasonal Antarctic ozone hole. Since the late 1970s two related phenomena have been observed: a lowered total amount of ozone in the upper stratosphere, and a much larger springtime decrease over the [[South Pole]]. The main cause is ozone-depleting substances such as chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), halons and HCFCs, used as refrigerants, solvents, propellants and foam-blowing agents. In the stratosphere they release halogen atoms, mainly [[Chlorine|chlorine]] and [[Bromine|bromine]], which catalyze the breakdown of ozone into oxygen. The ozone layer blocks harmful UVB light, whose increase is linked to [[Skin cancer|skin cancer]], sunburn and cataracts. The 1987 Montreal Protocol banned production of CFCs and halons, and its controls took effect in 1989. Ozone levels stabilized by the mid-1990s and began recovering in the 2000s. In 2019 NASA reported that the ozone hole was the smallest since its discovery in 1982.

Sonnet by the English Romantic poet [[Percy Bysshe Shelley|Percy Shelley]], first published on 11 January 1818 in *The Examiner*. Its subject is the Egyptian [[Pharaoh|pharaoh]] [[Ramesses II]], whose Greek name was Ozymandias. A traveler finds a shattered statue in the desert, its inscription boasting of the king's power, and "the lone and level sands stretch far away." Shelley began it in anticipation of the Younger Memnon, a statue fragment of Ramesses II that reached London in 1821. The poem grew out of a Christmas 1817 contest with Horace Smith, who wrote a sonnet of the same title.
